input: In this worked example, the goal is to compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and to determine the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant $k$ (min-1) fixes the half-life $t_{1/2}$ (min) by $t_{1/2} = \ln(2)/k$, and the fraction remaining after time $t$ (min) is $\exp(-k t)$. The measured rate constant in this case is $k$ = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. The worked results are a half-life of 10 min and a fraction remaining after 60 min of 0.02 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. In this particular case the measured value, namely $k$ = 0.069 min-1, is the single experimental input from which both of the requested quantities are obtained, and the care that was taken over its measurement, with readings spread across the full duration of the experiment, is what allows the two results to be stated with confidence. It is important to note that the relations hold for a first-order reaction only, and that a reaction of another order follows a different decay law, so the results should not be applied beyond the first-order case to which they properly belong.
target: Compute the half-life of a first-order reaction with rate constant $k$ = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant $k$ (min-1) fixes the half-life $t_{1/2}$ (min) by $t_{1/2} = \ln(2)/k$, and the fraction remaining after time $t$ (min) is $\exp(-k t)$. The rate constant was obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. Substitution of $k$ = 0.069 min-1 in the half-life relation gives a half-life of 10 min. Substitution in the decay relation at $t$ = 60 min gives a fraction remaining of 0.02, dimensionless. The two results are consistent with each other: the decay relation returns the half value at a time equal to the half-life, and the stated results satisfy that check. The rate constant rests on measurements spread across the whole decay rather than on a pair of readings, so the half-life derived from it is a property of the fitted decay and not of any single interval between readings. The example is worked at the temperature of the measurement throughout. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither result carries over: the half-life would depend on the starting concentration, and the fraction remaining would follow the decay law of that order instead.
